chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Sama'ah narrated from Salih ibn Khalid, from Abu Jamilah, from Abu Utaibah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him: 'A slave with whom I have a milk-kinship (radha') is permissible for me to sell.' He said: 'He is merely a slave; if you wish, you can sell him, and if you wish, you can keep him. But when a man owns both his parents, they are free (not slaves).'

Thus, there is nothing in it that contradicts what we mentioned, because the one whose ownership was permitted in this report is the brother, and we have previously established that this is permissible due to milk-kinship, just as it is permissible due to lineage. To further clarify this, here is what was narrated:

key_terms.اَلنَّسَبِ: Lineage; blood relationship, used here to compare the strength of milk-kinship.
key_terms.حُرَّانِ: Free; two people who are not slaves, possessing full legal status.
key_terms.رَضَاعٌ: Milk-kinship; a legal relationship established through breastfeeding that creates similar rights to blood lineage.
key_terms.مَمْلُوكٌ: Slave; a person owned by another, subject to the owner's disposal.

ai.seo_question: Can an owner sell a slave who is related to him through milk-kinship (radha')?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi uses this narration from Imam al-Sadiq to clarify the extent of ownership rights over a slave with milk-kinship, distinguishing it from the stronger bond of lineage. The Imam establishes that while the slave remains property, the specific condition of owning both parents triggers their emancipation, a nuance that resolves apparent contradictions in earlier juristic discussions. This highlights the Shia scholarly method of reconciling textual evidence by analyzing the precise conditions of kinship and ownership.
